01 / THE MISSION / 1972

Apollo 17 rover.

The last parking spot.

For three excursions, an electric rover helped Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt explore the Taurus–Littrow valley. Before departing, Cernan drove it to a final parking spot about 158 metres from the lunar module. Its television camera watched the astronauts lift off.

SCROLL TO CONTINUE ↓
THE MISSION ENDS. THE STORY CONTINUES.

What
remains.

The rover could not come home. It remains on the Moon, alongside the descent stage and equipment from the mission. The tracks are a record of where people went—and the samples they collected still give scientists new questions to ask.

02 / THE MISSION / 1967

Surveyor 3.

The explorer we went back to.

Before people stepped onto the Moon, Surveyor 3 tested its soil and sent back thousands of television images. Its sampler helped establish that the ground could support an Apollo lunar module. Contact ended on 4 May 1967.

SCROLL TO CONTINUE ↓
THE MISSION ENDS. THE STORY CONTINUES.

What
remains.

In November 1969, Apollo 12 astronauts walked to the silent lander. They removed its camera and other parts for study on Earth. The rest stayed behind. Surveyor 3 became a rare case of humans revisiting a robotic explorer on another world.

03 / THE MISSION / 2004—2018

Opportunity.

A short plan. An extraordinary life.

Opportunity arrived with a planned prime mission of 90 Martian days. It kept exploring for more than 14 Earth years, following clues to a wetter Mars across 45.16 kilometres of terrain. Then a planet-wide dust storm darkened the sky and cut its solar power.

SCROLL TO CONTINUE ↓
THE MISSION ENDS. THE STORY CONTINUES.

What
remains.

Its final signal reached Earth on 10 June 2018. Recovery attempts continued until NASA declared the mission complete in February 2019. The rover remains in Perseverance Valley. Its observations helped establish that ancient Mars had environments that could have supported microbial life—not that life was found.

04 / THE MISSION / 2004—2010

Spirit.

Even a broken wheel found a way.

Spirit explored Mars alongside its twin, Opportunity. A dragging wheel unexpectedly uncovered silica-rich soil—evidence consistent with ancient hot springs or steam vents. A mechanical problem had become a scientific opportunity.

SCROLL TO CONTINUE ↓
THE MISSION ENDS. THE STORY CONTINUES.

What
remains.

After becoming stuck in soft soil, Spirit continued working from one place. It fell silent in March 2010, and NASA ended recovery efforts in May 2011. The rover remains at Gusev crater, while its discoveries continue to shape our understanding of a once-wetter Mars.

05 / THE MISSION / 1976—1982

Viking 1.

A new world, at ground level.

Viking 1 brought the Martian surface into focus from a fixed landing site. Its cameras, weather instruments, and biology experiments made the lander a laboratory on another planet, paired with an orbiter overhead.

SCROLL TO CONTINUE ↓
THE MISSION ENDS. THE STORY CONTINUES.

What
remains.

The lander operated until November 1982, far beyond its original mission. Its biology experiments did not establish that life existed on Mars. Viking’s results helped define the questions that later missions would pursue. The lander remains in Chryse Planitia.

06 / THE MISSION / 2018—2022

InSight.

It stayed still. And looked deeper.

InSight did not need to drive. From Elysium Planitia, it placed instruments on the ground and listened for seismic activity. By recording marsquakes, it helped scientists investigate the structure hidden beneath the surface.

SCROLL TO CONTINUE ↓
THE MISSION ENDS. THE STORY CONTINUES.

What
remains.

Dust on the solar panels gradually reduced the power available to the lander, and the mission ended in December 2022. Its instruments remain on Mars. The measurements it returned continue to offer a way to look inside a planet we have barely touched.
